title: Search and Passage Are Decoupled for Migrating Trout Kelts at Multi‐Exit Dam
content:
ABSTRACT

Longitudinal and lateral river connectivity have been drastically reduced over time, with hydropower development as a major driver of fragmentation. While fishways are widely implemented to support upstream migration, downstream passage remains a major challenge. For salmonids, most downstream studies focus on juvenile fish, while post-spawning adults (kelts) have received less attention. Here, we studied the forebay behaviour and downstream route choice of brown trout (Salmo trutta) kelts at a run-of-the-river hydropower plant with multiple passage options using hydroacoustic telemetry. Kelts spent an average of 9 days in the forebay, with strongly right-skewed residence times. Activity was approximately uniform across the diel period. Swimming depth was generally mid-water to deep (median depth 3.9 m), and kelts were deeper during daytime, during upstream-directed movement and at higher river discharge. Kelts switched between shallow and deep positions more often during night than day, and much more during up- and downstream movement than during episodes when horizontal movement was limited. Encounters with potential passage routes were not proportional to discharge distribution: spillways were underrepresented, whereas the fishway and ice gate were overrepresented. Once a kelt encountered a route, passage probability was higher at night than during the day, increased with higher mean opening velocity, and was higher for openings closer to the surface. Inter-individual variation was substantial across analyses. Our results provide information for the design and operation of downstream-passage measures for large-bodied post-spawners.
